newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- MAY 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- MAY 16.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The government is opening the way for a discussion of the country's social security and pension system alongside possible changes to the job market during its social dialogue with unions and employers. A meeting of ruling PASOK party and government officials last night it was decided to introduce minor issues gradually into the dialogue.

--Cyprus and Greek-Turkish relations were the focus of last night's meeting between Prime Minister Costas Simitis, Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos and Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos. The Greek expert committee on Greek-Turkish relations, government sources said, will submit its memorandum to the Dutch EU presidency mid-June and no earlier.

--Ruling PASOK MPs forced Interior Minister Alekos Papadopoulos to beat a hurried retreat with his bill to end the garbage collectors' strike by acceding to their demand for permanent positions. Dissenting MPs said the move would simply rubber stamp illegal actions by municipalities. Rubbish on the streets of Athens continues to pile up.
--Plans for a concert by teen idols Sakis Rouvas and his Turkish counterpart Burat Cut have not been derailed by criticism in Greece and Cyprus over the event's "apolitical" nature.

--Conservative opposition New Democracy deputies are still smarting over former premier George Rallis's comments this week praising the government's policies. The government however was more than happy to welcome it.
--After 72 years on the high street, Akron Illion Crystal was forced to shut down with debts of four billion drachmas.

--The government is preparing to levy a circulation charge on all secondhand cars - whether imported or not - as it appears the European Court will rule against Greece later this month for imposing a special charge on imported secondhand cars. The measure will be one of four the government is planning for next year, to recoup losses if the Court ruling goes against Greece.

--The Ionian Bank has found more than 1,000 priceless ancient Roman and Greek coins and other valuable items, unclaimed by the owner "Kalogeropoulos" who has to be sighted since 1920, according to reports. The bank is considering displaying the treasures at its Corfu museum.
--The government is planning to get around losing its tax on imported secondhand cars by imposing an "environment tax" on all car purchasers.

--Late PASOK founder Andrea Papandreou's widow, Dimitra Liani shook off the injunctions and writs regarding the status of her villa and went to meet the people at the National Garden's Book Fair last night.
--Yesterday's mutiny by PASOK MPs against the government conceals greater problems within the ruling party that may tie up the government's work. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
